topic: Agent Goal Hijacking: Top OWASP Agentic AI Risk Explained

key_points: Canonical OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 source that ranks ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack as the first agentic risk.
Frames agentic risk around autonomous systems that plan, act, and make decisions across workflows.
Positions the list as globally peer-reviewed and developed with more than 100 experts, researchers, and practitioners.
Defines ASI01 as attackers altering agent objectives or decision paths through malicious content.
Gives concrete attack scenarios: gradual plan injection, direct instruction injection, unauthorized tool chains, and reflection-loop traps.
Useful for a practical testing section because Promptfoo maps the risk to red-team cases.
Explains Agent Goal Hijack and Tool Misuse as direct-action hijacking risks.
Emphasizes that agents struggle to distinguish trusted instructions from malicious payloads hidden in pages, files, or tool outputs.
Strong identity/security angle: agent risk becomes worse when agents inherit user privileges or access enterprise systems.
Focuses on containment: prompt injection may still occur, but blast radius should be bounded by permissions, approved tools, argument validation, and policy checks.
Good counterpoint to purely detection-based advice because it recommends least privilege and scoped tool access.
Useful for sections on implementation controls for SaaS and enterprise developers.
Covers observed web-based indirect prompt injection against AI agents and distinguishes real-world attacks from theoretical worst cases.
Notes that many observed cases are still opportunistic or low-impact, which creates a useful nuance for threat modeling.
Good source for explaining why teams should prioritize browser, RAG, email, document, and external-web ingestion paths.
Explains goal hijacking for IT and identity teams, with indirect prompt injection as the primary delivery vector.
Describes hidden commands in PDFs, web results, and other external resources that agents read during normal tasks.
Useful for a plain-English definition and IAM-oriented mitigation framing.

stats.fact: OWASP describes the Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 as a globally peer-reviewed framework built with input from more than 100 industry experts, researchers, and practitioners.
Darktrace's State of AI Cybersecurity 2026 reported that 92% of security professionals are concerned about the impact of AI agents.
Okta reported that 69% of surveyed enterprise buyers say security concerns are slowing AI-agent adoption, and 57% characterize securing disparate agents, apps, and workflows as a high-effort problem.
IBM survey coverage reported that AI-agent use is expected to grow 38% by 2027, while 77% of technology leaders say current governance frameworks are inadequate.

The State of AI Agent Security 2026 report found that 19.5% of CISOs surveyed had experienced at least one AI-agent-related security incident, including prompt injection, plugin data exposure, and unauthorized actions.

Recorded Future cited Gartner's prediction that as many as 40% of enterprise applications will include task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, and Deloitte's expectation that at least 75% of companies will use agentic AI to some extent by 2028.

Help Net Security coverage reported that multi-turn prompt-injection and jailbreak testing across eight open-weight models reached success rates as high as 92%, highlighting why longer agent sessions need controls beyond single-turn filters.

angles: Lead with the distinction between prompt injection and goal hijacking: prompt injection changes an instruction, while goal hijacking redirects an autonomous workflow that can call tools and affect real systems.
Frame ASI01 as a control-plane problem for agents: separate trusted instructions, untrusted content, tools, memory, and identity instead of relying on model behavior alone.

Use a developer-focused attack path: attacker plants hidden instructions in a web page, ticket, PDF, email, or RAG document; the agent reads it; the agent changes plan; the agent calls tools with user or service privileges.

Contrast theoretical risk with current observed attacks: real-world cases are emerging and sometimes low impact, but the damage curve changes when agents get credentials, browser access, code execution, or production APIs.
Connect ASI01 to adjacent OWASP risks: Tool Misuse, Identity & Privilege Abuse, Memory & Context Poisoning, and Insecure Inter-Agent Communication often turn a goal hijack into a real breach.

Offer a mitigation stack developers can implement: permission scoping, tool allowlists, argument schemas, policy gates, human approval for high-impact actions, untrusted-content labeling, runtime monitoring, and red-team tests.
Include an enterprise buyer angle: security concerns are now slowing agent adoption, so product teams that ship agent isolation, audit logs, policy controls, and identity governance can win trust.
